source.title: Athletic Performance at the National Basketball Association Combine After Anterior Cruciate Ligament Reconstruction

paper.citation: Mehran, N., Williams, P. N., Keller, R. A., Khalil, L. S., Lombardo, S. J., & Kharrazi, F. D. (2016). Athletic performance at the National Basketball Association Combine after anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction. Orthopaedic Journal of Sports Medicine, 4(5), 2325967116648083. https://doi.org/10.1177/2325967116648083
paper.abstract: Do NBA Combine speed, agility, and jump results differ between athletes with prior primary ACL reconstruction and age-, size-, position-, and combine-year-matched controls without reported knee surgery? Investigators reviewed 1,092 NBA Combine invitees from 2000–2015 and identified 21 athletes who participated after primary ACL reconstruction. Four additional reconstructed athletes withdrew because surgery occurred too close to the combine, underscoring that the analyzed group had already achieved a high return-to-performance threshold. Each ACL-reconstructed athlete was matched to one control; the mean time from reconstruction to combine was 2 years (range 1–5). Retrospective matched case-control study based on public sources for surgical history and official NBA Combine data. Outcomes were lane agility, shuttle run, three-quarter-court sprint, standing vertical jump, and maximum vertical jump. Groups were matched by combine year, position, age, height, and weight; Wilcoxon-Mann-Whitney tests addressed small samples.
paper.tldr: This paper provides a narrowly defined comparison of combine performance among elite basketball prospects who had already returned to a high level after ACL reconstruction. No combine outcome differed statistically between the 21 ACL-reconstructed athletes and 21 controls. Interpretation should remain within the reviewed population, design, and applicability limits.
paper.methods: Retrospective matched case-control study based on public sources for surgical history and official NBA Combine data. Outcomes were lane agility, shuttle run, three-quarter-court sprint, standing vertical jump, and maximum vertical jump. Groups were matched by combine year, position, age, height, and weight; Wilcoxon-Mann-Whitney tests addressed small samples.
paper.findings: No combine outcome differed statistically between the 21 ACL-reconstructed athletes and 21 controls. Mean lane-agility time was 11.5 seconds in both groups (p=.745), shuttle time 3.1 seconds in both (p=.346), and three-quarter-court sprint time 3.3 seconds in both (p=.516). Maximum vertical jump averaged 33.6 inches after reconstruction versus 33.9 inches in controls (p=.548). Standing vertical jump averaged 28.2 versus 29.2 inches (p=.067); this non-significant one-inch difference should not be interpreted as evidence of equivalence.
paper.limitations: Retrospective public-data ascertainment may misclassify surgical history; medical charts, injury details, concomitant pathology, graft technique, surgeon, rehabilitation, and postoperative course were unavailable. Strong survivor/selection bias limits inference: only prospects good enough to earn a combine invitation and healthy enough to participate were analyzed. The study was small and likely underpowered for modest differences, particularly the standing-jump comparison. Bilateral combine tests do not capture limb asymmetry, movement quality, strength, symptoms, reinjury risk, or readiness for an individual athlete. Findings apply to selected elite male basketball prospects and cannot establish that ACL reconstruction has no performance cost in broader athlete populations.
paper.practicalImplications: The results support the possibility that highly selected basketball prospects can regain combine-level outputs after ACL reconstruction. They do not justify using group-average combine scores as return-to-sport clearance criteria. Preserve individualized assessment of symptoms, exposure tolerance, unilateral performance, movement strategy, and reinjury risk.
paper.athleteDev: For athlete-development decisions, use this evidence only within the reviewed population and context. The results support the possibility that highly selected basketball prospects can regain combine-level outputs after ACL reconstruction. They do not justify using group-average combine scores as return-to-sport clearance criteria. Preserve individualized assessment of symptoms, exposure tolerance, unilateral performance, movement strategy, and reinjury risk. Do not treat the study as a universal development pathway or benchmark.
paper.rtp: For rehabilitation and return-to-sport decisions, the results support the possibility that highly selected basketball prospects can regain combine-level outputs after ACL reconstruction. They do not justify using group-average combine scores as return-to-sport clearance criteria. Preserve individualized assessment of symptoms, exposure tolerance, unilateral performance, movement strategy, and reinjury risk. This study alone does not establish clearance criteria or a complete return-to-sport progression.
